name: liblouis
why: Braille translation and back-translation is a fascinating transform between text and tactile code, with a rich table-driven design behind it.

brief.what_it_is: Liblouis is an open-source braille translator and back-translator, a C library that converts text into braille and braille back into text. It supports computer and literary braille, contracted and uncontracted translation for many languages, hyphenation, and math braille (Nemeth and Marburg). Translation rules live in table files, and the library is distributed as a shared library on Linux and macOS and as a DLL on Windows. The package also includes command-line tools (lou_allround, lou_checkhyphens, lou_checktable, lou_debug, lou_translate, lou_trace) for testing and debugging translation tables. A companion project, Liblouisutdml, adds a formatter that turns XML or plain text into embosser-ready braille.
brief.why_it_exists: The project is named in honor of Louis Braille and aims to provide braille translation for many languages and braille codes as a free library that applications can embed. The README says it is based on the translation routines in the BRLTTY screenreader and has 'gone far beyond these routines'. Its screen-reader support is a stated purpose: it is used by NVDA and Orca and in commercial products such as ViewPlus.
brief.how_it_works: Translation is table-driven: new languages are added through tables that support rule-based or dictionary-based approaches, and the repository ships tables for many languages (en-us-g2.ctb and en-us-g1.ctb are named as examples). The library is written in C so it needs no runtime and can be called from Python, Java, and JavaScript bindings. Back-translation uses the same tables in reverse, and the included tools test and trace those translations.

brief.install_notes: Not a brew-only install. The README describes unpacking the release tarball from GitHub Releases, then running ./configure, make, and sudo make install, with sudo ldconfig possibly needed afterwards. Optional extras are help2man for man pages and libyaml for the extended test suite. Other installation routes are described in the HACKING file, which the README points to. Windows builds are a DLL, and the README does not give a Windows install walkthrough.
brief.standout: Translation rules are data in table files rather than hard-coded logic, so one engine covers many languages and braille codes, and new languages can be added through tables. It also ships back-translation and a set of table-testing and tracing tools, which is less common than forward translation alone. The library's clean C interface means it can be called from many language bindings and is embedded in screen readers and in Bookshare's book production.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage lists Liblouis Release 3.39.0 dated 01 Sep 2026 and 3.38.0 dated 01 Jun 2026, and a louis-rs 0.3.0 Rust reimplementation dated 22 Sep 2026. The README links a release schedule on the wiki. I did not check the repository commit history.
brief.caveats: The library is licensed under LGPLv2.1+, but the command-line tools are GPLv3+, which the README states separately. Building from source is the documented route, with a 16-bit Unicode default and a configure option for 32-bit. The homepage's 3.39.0 notes say the spacing parameter of the translation functions has been deprecated. The README mentions that the tool-side documentation lives on the separate liblouis.io site, and I did not fetch it. The brew entry has no caveats.

entry.title: liblouis
entry.tldr: A table-driven braille translator that turns text into braille and back again, the engine inside screen readers like NVDA and Orca.
entry.deeper_look:
Liblouis is a C library that converts text to braille and braille back to text. It handles computer braille and literary braille, contracted and uncontracted, for many languages, plus hyphenation and math codes (Nemeth and Marburg). It is named in honor of Louis Braille.

The rules are not hard-coded. They live in table files, such as `en-us-g2.ctb` and `en-us-g1.ctb`, and one engine reads whichever table you point it at. New languages and braille codes are added by writing tables that use a rule-based or dictionary-based approach. Back-translation runs on the same tables in reverse.

The project grew out of the translation routines in the BRLTTY screen reader and, in the README's words, has 'gone far beyond these routines'. It is used by NVDA and Orca and in commercial products such as ViewPlus. Because it is plain C with no runtime, it can be called from Python, Java and JavaScript bindings.

The command-line tools are the part to play with. `lou_translate` converts text, while `lou_trace`, `lou_debug`, `lou_checktable` and `lou_checkhyphens` exist for testing and debugging tables. Braille contractions are a lot like a compression scheme with context-dependent rules, and the tools let you watch those rules fire.
entry.install:
brew install liblouis
# Homebrew pulls in python@3.15. The upstream README describes a source build instead: ./configure, make, sudo make install, then sudo ldconfig if needed.

entry.whats_unique: Braille rules are data in table files, so one engine covers many languages and codes. It also ships back-translation and table-debugging tools, which is less common than forward translation alone.
entry.caveats: The brief did not cover the tools' usage, so check the liblouis.io documentation for table names and options; the library is LGPL but the command-line tools are GPLv3+.
